mean: the feeling a voice or message carries, like friendly, cold or angry
ex: Nobody minded what Meera said in the meeting; it was her sharp tone that hurt the team.
ex2: On the family WhatsApp group, Dadi read Rahul's one-word reply and asked why his tone was so cold.
note: Text messages lose tone easily; a short 'ok' can sound angry even when it is not meant that way.

mean: saying the opposite of what you mean, to mock or show annoyance
ex: When the train was two hours late, Arjun said 'Wonderful service!' in a sarcastic voice, and the platform laughed.
ex2: After India lost the toss again, Fatima's sarcastic 'Great luck, as always' made her brother groan.
note: Sarcasm is hard to read in text; people often add an emoji so it is not taken literally.

mean: the reason why someone does something
ex: When the neighbour suddenly brought sweets, Lata guessed his motive: he wanted her parking spot.
ex2: The police in Lucknow are still trying to understand the motive behind the bank fraud.
note: Motive is the reason inside a person; 'motivation' is the drive to act. Police look for a 'motive' for a crime.

mean: to praise someone too much, often to get something from them
ex: Before asking for leave, Sunil likes to flatter his boss about her excellent presentation.
ex2: The sari seller tried to flatter Aunty by saying she looked twenty-five, hoping she would buy two.
note: 'I'm flattered' is a polite way to accept a compliment; to flatter someone usually means praise that is not fully sincere.

mean: what your face, hands and posture show about your feelings
ex: Priya said she was fine, but her body language, arms crossed and eyes down, told a different story.
ex2: In the interview, Karan's calm body language made the panel trust him before he had said much.
note: Body language gives clues, not proof; crossed arms can also simply mean someone is cold.

mean: quick to protect yourself, as if every question is an attack
ex: When the coach asked about the dropped catch, Vikram got defensive and blamed the floodlights.
ex2: Ask Mama a simple question about the electricity bill and he becomes defensive about his spending.
note: Getting defensive often means a question touched a sore spot, but it can also mean someone feels unfairly blamed.

mean: to understand and share how another person feels
ex: Having failed her own first attempt, Anjali could empathise with students who cried after the NEET results.
ex2: A good doctor will empathise with a scared patient before explaining the treatment.
note: Empathise means feeling with someone; sympathise means feeling sorry for them. Always 'empathise with'.

mean: to turn attention away from a question or blame onto something else
ex: Asked about the delayed bridge, the official tried to deflect by talking about last year's rains.
ex2: When Amma asked who broke the vase, Chintu tried to deflect by pointing at the cat.
note: In debates, watch for answers that deflect: the speaker replies to a different question from the one asked.

mean: to sense the mood of a group and act to suit it
ex: At the condolence meeting, Naveen didn't read the room and started talking about his new car.
ex2: Good stand-up comics in Bengaluru read the room and quickly drop jokes that are not landing.
note: Often used in the negative: 'He couldn't read the room' means he said something badly timed.

mean: to say hurtful things to provoke or mock someone
ex: The away fans kept trying to taunt the bowler, but he calmly took two wickets in the next over.
ex2: Relatives at the wedding would taunt Sneha about her job, so she stayed near the food stall.
note: In Indian English 'taunt' often means any sarcastic remark; in standard English it is more deliberately hurtful.

mean: messages that seem to mean two opposite things
ex: My manager praises my work but never gives me bigger projects; I'm getting mixed signals.
ex2: The weather office sent mixed signals, warning of heavy rain while saying schools could stay open.
note: Usually plural: 'mixed signals', not 'a mixed signal'.

mean: the real meaning under the words, which is not said directly
ex: Neha's aunt said 'Your cooking is so modern', and the subtext was clear: she missed the old recipes.
ex2: Read the subtext of the company memo: 'restructuring' probably means some people will lose their jobs.
note: Subtext is the meaning beneath the words; context is the situation around them. Do not mix them up.

mean: showing anger indirectly, through hints, silence or sly remarks, not openly
ex: Instead of asking us to wash up, our flatmate left a passive-aggressive note: 'Hope you enjoyed MY clean plates.'
ex2: Writing 'As per my last email' can sound passive-aggressive, even if Divya only meant to remind her colleague.
note: It describes behaviour, not a fixed type of person; most of us do it sometimes. Saying 'I'm upset that...' is clearer.

mean: a hidden reason for doing something, different from the one you show
ex: Rakesh suddenly offered to help with my tax return, and I wondered if he had an ulterior motive.
ex2: The panchayat suspected an ulterior motive when the builder offered a free school building near the lake.
note: Almost always negative: it suggests selfish plans behind kind actions.

mean: praise that hides an insult inside it
ex: 'You look nice today, for once,' said Sonia, a backhanded compliment that ruined Pooja's morning.
ex2: Calling the new batsman 'surprisingly good for a small-town boy' was a backhanded compliment, and the commentator apologised.
note: Watch for 'for a...': 'Not bad for a beginner' is a typical backhanded compliment.

mean: a question that hides an unfair claim, so any answer seems to admit it
ex: The anchor asked a loaded question: 'Why does your department keep wasting public money?'
ex2: 'Have you stopped copying in exams?' is a loaded question, because yes or no both make Ravi look guilty.
note: A trick question tests cleverness; a loaded question sneaks in an accusation. Answer by challenging the hidden claim.

mean: to control or influence people unfairly, often without them noticing
ex: Some fake job agents manipulate young people by promising Gulf visas and then demanding huge fees.
ex2: Ishaan's friend would manipulate him with guilt: 'After everything I've done, you can't lend me your bike?'
note: Persuading is open and leaves the choice to you; manipulating uses tricks, guilt or lies to steer you.

mean: to make someone doubt their own memory or sense of reality, usually over time
ex: Her manager would gaslight Nisha, denying instructions he had clearly given, until she started recording every meeting.
ex2: A Pune counsellor explained that to gaslight someone is to deny the truth repeatedly until they stop trusting their own memory.
note: It means a repeated pattern of making someone doubt reality. A single lie or an honest disagreement is not gaslighting.

mean: a way of describing facts that makes them look better than they are
ex: The company called the layoffs 'right-sizing', but the employees saw it as pure spin.
ex2: After the heavy defeat, the captain's spin was that the young players had 'gained valuable experience'.
note: In cricket, spin is a bowling style; in news and PR it means presenting facts in a favourable light.

mean: to make someone feel guilty so that they do what you want
ex: Every Diwali, Bua tries to guilt-trip Aman: 'You never visit, so we must be unimportant to you.'
ex2: Some shopping apps guilt-trip users with buttons like 'No thanks, I don't like saving money.'
note: As a noun it is often written without a hyphen: 'Don't lay a guilt trip on me.'

mean: expressed indirectly, but still clear enough to be understood
ex: The landlord's message, 'Many people want this flat', was a veiled threat to raise Rohit's rent.
ex2: In his speech, the cricket board chief made a veiled reference to players who skip domestic matches.
note: 'Thinly veiled' means the hint is very easy to see: 'thinly veiled anger'.

mean: a false reason given to hide the real reason for doing something
ex: Using a fake office call as a pretext, Deepak left the wedding early to watch the match.
ex2: The neighbour came to borrow sugar, but it was a pretext to find out why the police had visited.
note: Use 'on/under the pretext of + -ing': 'He called on the pretext of asking about my health.'

mean: an indirect remark that suggests something bad, usually about someone
ex: There was no proof against the treasurer, only innuendo spread through the housing society's WhatsApp group.
ex2: The film was criticised for jokes full of innuendo that made families in the hall uncomfortable.
note: It often hints at something improper or sexual. Innuendo is not proof; it works only by suggestion.

mean: so friendly or honest that people stop feeling suspicious or angry
ex: The angry customer calmed down at once because of the young waiter's disarming honesty about the mistake.
ex2: Nanaji has a disarming smile that makes even grumpy shopkeepers in Chandni Chowk give him a discount.
note: Disarming charm can be genuine or a tactic; reading people means noticing which one it is.
